items.title: LeanCPMS documentation
items.text:
LeanCPMS is an open-source charge point management system (CPMS) for EV charging: small, complete, and debuggable. These pages are for the people who use an instance of it, such as LeanCPMS Cloud, and for developers who build on it. The product itself is described at leancpms.com.

LeanCPMS is pre-release. These pages describe the code as it is; where something is not built yet, they say so.

items.title: Guides
items.text:
• Users and access: people, organizations, roles and API keys, how to log in to the portal and with cpms login, and the common tasks of an organization's administrator.
  • The command line: installing cpms (uv tool install leancpms-cli), configuring it, managing an organization's YAML documents from a git repository, and using it from scripts and agents.

items.title: Driver API
items.text: • The driver flow and the driver API: drop-in charging by QR code step by step, and /api/driver/v1/, the API for an organization's own driver front end.

items.title: Design
items.text: How the system is laid out, and why, will be published here: the architecture and the product requirements, written for readers outside the project. They are not public yet.

items.title: Source
items.text: The source code is licensed under AGPL-3.0. The repository is private until the system runs; the command line is published on PyPI as leancpms-cli.

items.title: cpms, the LeanCPMS command line
items.text:
cpms manages an organization in a LeanCPMS instance from your own machine: live state, sessions, the monthly settlements, and the declared state (organization, price list, sites) as YAML documents you can keep in a git repository. It talks to the instance's JSON API over HTTPS with an API key, and the same commands work for people and for AI agents.

This directory builds leancpms-cli, the command without the server. It depends on httpx, pydantic and PyYAML only.

items.title: Install
items.text:
With uv, from PyPI:

uv tool install leancpms-cli
cpms --help

That needs no access to the repository. With access, also from a GitHub release (a tag cli-v<version>) or straight from the repository:

gh release download cli-v0.1.4 --repo forsslund/leancpms --pattern '*.whl'
uv tool install ./leancpms_cli-0.1.4-py3-none-any.whl
# or
uv tool install "git+https://github.com/forsslund/leancpms#subdirectory=cli"
  • The repository is private for now, so these two need read access to it on GitHub; over SSH the URL is git+ssh://git@github.com/forsslund/leancpms#subdirectory=cli.
  • It needs Python 3.14. uv downloads it if your machine lacks it.
  • To get a newer version, run uv tool upgrade leancpms-cli. To pin a version, add @<tag or commit> after the repository URL.
  • pipx install "git+…#subdirectory=cli" works too.
  • Do not install it into an environment that already has the server (leancpms). The server already includes cpms, and both packages carry the same files, so uninstalling one breaks the other.

items.title: Configure
items.text:
Log in with the same e-mail address you use for the instance's portal:

cpms login --url https://cpms.example.com

It prints a code and opens the portal's page for it in your browser (or prints the address only: --no-browser, or no display). Log in there if you are not, check that the page shows the same code, choose your organization and whether the key may act (write) or only look (read), and approve. Your role as a member decides which you may choose: members are read unless the operator, or a colleague with a write key, made them write (cpms members set-role). cpms login waits for that and then saves a personal key, yours and that organization's, as the profile [default] (--profile NAME for another) in ~/.config/cpms/config.toml, readable only by you. Other profiles in the file stay as they were.

cpms whoami      # which key is in use, whose, for which organization
cpms logout      # revokes the key on the server and removes the profile

The key stops working when you are removed as a member, and so does every key you issued with it. Approve a code only if you just ran cpms login yourself: whoever started it gets the key. docs/users-and-access.md explains members, roles and keys in full, with several computers, a lost computer, and common tasks.

items.title: Machine keys, for CI and agents
items.text:
A pipeline or an agent of its own gets a machine key instead, which records who issued it: cpms keys issue --name ci --scope read with your personal write key. It is shown only once. An organization key sees only its own organization. A key you issue lives only as long as your membership: when you leave, it is revoked with your own. An integration that must outlive you gets its key from the operator. Members you add do stay when you leave; cpms members list shows who added whom.

Put the URL and the key in ~/.config/cpms/config.toml (or $XDG_CONFIG_HOME/cpms/, or the path in CPMS_CONFIG), readable only by you (chmod 600):

[default]
url = "https://cpms.example.com"
api_key = "lcp_…"

[test]
url = "http://localhost:8000"
api_key = "lcp_…"

Alternatively, set CPMS_URL and CPMS_API_KEY in the environment, which suits CI and agents. --profile test (or CPMS_PROFILE=test) picks a profile. Without a profile, the environment wins, then [default]. A networked command that has neither exits 2 and says what to set.

items.title: Use
items.text:
cpms                                      # live state: sites, fuse groups, outlets, current per phase
cpms sessions --since 2026-10-01
cpms report settlements --month 2026-10   # the month's settlements per site, with bookkeeping proposals
cpms manifest export acme > all.yaml
cpms manifest export acme --site main-street > sites/main-street.yaml
cpms manifest validate sites/main-street.yaml   # offline: the schema
cpms manifest plan sites/main-street.yaml       # the server: the diff, references, live warnings
cpms manifest apply sites/main-street.yaml -m "Fused up to 50 A"
cpms manifest history acme --site main-street

cpms --help and cpms manifest --help list the rest.

items.title: A repository of manifests
items.text:
One file per document works well:

organization.yaml
pricelist.yaml
sites/main-street.yaml
sites/harbour.yaml

Edit a file, run validate and plan, commit, then run apply with the commit's reason as -m. The server holds the truth and the files are a way to say things: if someone changed a price in the portal, plan shows that applying your file would undo it, and export brings the file up to date. apply refuses a document that changed on the server since your plan; plan again. Removing anything needs --prune. validate needs no key, so CI can run it on every pull request; plan needs one.

An outlet's public_id is the id in its QR code (/c/<public_id>). Leave it out and the server makes one up on first apply and keeps it. Once the codes are printed, write the ids into the site file (- {connector: 1, key: s1-1, public_id: h7k2m9pq}): a declared id applies, also on a new server, and plan warns before an outlet's id changes.

items.title: In your editor: the JSON Schema
items.text:
The documents have a JSON Schema, so an editor can complete field names and flag mistakes as you type. That works in editors that use yaml-language-server: VS Code with Red Hat's YAML extension, Neovim, Helix, Zed. Add this line at the top of each file:

# yaml-language-server: $schema=https://raw.githubusercontent.com/forsslund/leancpms/main/schema/manifest.cpms-v1.schema.json

That URL works once the repository is public; replace main with a tag to pin a version. Until then, use a local copy, written by the command itself and kept in your manifest repository:

cpms manifest schema > cpms-v1.schema.json

# yaml-language-server: $schema=../cpms-v1.schema.json

The path is relative to the YAML file. export does not write the line, so add it again after an export.

The schema checks types, required and unknown fields, allowed values, key spelling, and that amounts are quoted ("4.70", not 4.70). It does not check anything that spans several fields: a budget above the fuse, duplicate keys, ocpp ids or public ids, a plan naming a missing tariff, or an unknown time zone. validate and plan check those. Only plan knows whether another outlet on the server already has a public id.

items.title: For agents
items.text:
• --json works on every command, before or after the subcommand.
  • Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 the action failed (the server said no, the server could not be reached, a plan has errors), 2 usage or configuration.
  • cpms manifest apply never prompts without a TTY. It prints the plan and exits 2 unless you pass --yes. Show the plan to a person first, then apply with --yes -m "why".
  • session … stop|close acts at once, with no confirmation step.
  • Pass the key in the environment or the config file, never on the command line or in a transcript.

items.title: Releasing (maintainers)
items.text:
Raise version in both cli/pyproject.toml and the root pyproject.toml (a test keeps them equal), then tag and push:

git tag cli-v0.1.4 && git push origin cli-v0.1.4

.github/workflows/release-cli.yml builds the wheel and sdist, smoke-tests the wheel, and attaches both to a GitHub release. It also publishes to PyPI when the repository variable PYPI_PUBLISH is true. That needs, once: a PyPI account with two-factor authentication; a pending trusted publisher on PyPI for the project leancpms-cli (owner forsslund, repository leancpms, workflow release-cli.yml, environment pypi); and an environment pypi in the GitHub repository's settings. A pending publisher does not reserve the name: if someone else registers leancpms-cli first, it becomes invalid. The first release creates the project and so reserves the name. Trusted publishing uses GitHub's OIDC token, so no PyPI token is stored anywhere. A file published to PyPI cannot be replaced, only yanked: a wrong release is fixed with a new version.

items.title: The driver flow (cpms/driver/)
items.text: Drop-in charging for a driver with no account, no app and no login (PRD §2, architecture §3): scan the static QR code, see the price, pay by card, plug in, watch, stop, get a receipt. Goal: QR → charging in under a minute on a phone.

items.title: Pages
items.text:
URL What / only on a host in an organization's driver_hosts: its published sites, each with its public outlets, their live status (the QR page's badge) and a link to /c/<public_id>. The ad hoc price incl. VAT once at the top. HTMX polls every 30 s. A 404 on any other host. /c/<public_id> the QR code (Outlet.public_id: declared in the site document, or generated on first apply; stable across applies). Station, charge point, outlet, live status, the ad hoc price incl. VAT and the amount reserved, shown before anything starts (AFIR). E-mail for the receipt, accept, optionally "Start later" at a time of day, continue to payment. provider's page Stripe Checkout (or /pay/fake/<ref> in development) reserves the amount. /s/<token> the live page. Waiting for the payment → "plug in the cable" (with the time left) → "checking that the cable is locked" → kW, kWh, cost so far incl. VAT, Stop (or, scheduled: "charging starts at 23:00", start now, cancel) → finishing → done, with the receipt. A failed start is said here at once. HTMX polls every 3 s. /s/<token>/receipt the receipt (seller = the organization). Also e-mailed.

<token> is a capability: 24 random bytes, the only key to that one charge. A reloaded page, a locked phone or a second device finds the charge again with the link, and the receipt mail links back to it. The outlet page also remembers the browser's own active charge for a day (a signed cookie per outlet) and offers "show my charge".

Swedish first (LANGUAGE_CODE = "sv"), English available from the footer. Strings are English in the source; the catalog is cpms/locale/sv/LC_MESSAGES/django.po, maintained with uv run python scripts/messages.py (no GNU gettext needed; --check lists anything untranslated).

items.title: What happens, step by step
items.text:
Views are thin; every change is an action in services.py, journaled in the actions journal (never with the e-mail address, the tag or the token). Everything after the payment page is done by the worker (uv run manage.py worker), so it happens whether or not the driver's phone is still on the page.

  1. Begin (driver_begin). The outlet must be public, priced (the price list's ad hoc channel, flat tariffs only for now) and free: cpms's own read models first, then a live GET /chargers/{id} to ocpp-rest (responsive? this connector free?) right before any money is reserved. A DropIn row is created with the price shown, and the provider's checkout is opened for the plan's preauth_amount.
  2. Payment confirmed (driver_confirm_payment). Triggered by the provider's webhook (stored in the inbox, processed by the worker), by the driver's return (the worker asks the provider a couple of seconds later), or by a once-a-minute check. Each asks the provider directly; the driver's browser is never trusted. The authorization becomes a ledger Payment.
  3. Start (driver_start). A one-time id_tag (DRP + 17 random characters, 20 in total: the OCPP limit) is pushed with PUT /authorizations/{id_tag} scoped to this one box and expiring after the plug-in window, then POST …/connectors/{n}/start. The Aura then waits for the cable.
  4. Track (worker, every second). The session is found as consumer.Session with this box and this id_tag (a session the consumer attributes to another organization is never taken). If the gateway missed the session_start and the session was learned without a tag, the one learned session on this outlet since our start is taken, and only if there is exactly one.
    • No session within DRIVER_PLUG_TIMEOUT_S (default 180 s; it must be longer than ocpp-rest's REMOTE_START_GRACE_S, 120 s): the tag is revoked first, then the reservation is released.
    • The cost reaches the reservation: the worker sends one RemoteStop.
    • The session ends, by our Stop or because the driver unplugged: the drop-in is ended.
    • A session that appears after we gave up (the box started anyway) is stopped: the unpaid-session guard.
  5. Settle (settle_payment, in cpms/ledger/). After DRIVER_SETTLE_DELAY_S (30 s) from a definitive session_end, or DRIVER_SETTLE_DELAY_INFERRED_S (300 s) from an inferred one (a definitive end with the box's own meter value may follow), the session's amount_incl_vat is captured, capped at the authorization; 0 kWh (or anything below the provider's minimum) cancels instead. If the consumer could not price the session, the price shown to the driver is used.
  6. Receipt mail and tag revocation. At least once; a crash between sending and recording resends the same receipt (same number).

items.title: Scheduled start (PRD §6, slice 3a)
items.text:
"Start later" on the outlet page takes a time of day in the organization's time zone, the next time the clock shows it; services.begin takes any start_at (the driver API passes it on). The session starts at once, exactly as without it: the RemoteStart carries a limit of 0 A, which ocpp-rest puts into the first TxProfile, so the cable locks while the driver is at the car and no energy flows. The balancer is the scheduler (architecture §9): it reads start_at from GET /api/v1/balancer/sessions, keeps the session at 0 A until then and gives it its share from the next cycle after (cpms/balancer/README.md). The drop-in is scheduled from the session's start until start_at, then charging.

  • Start now sets start_at to now; cancel stops the session (0 Wh, the reservation is released, no failed-start notice: she cancelled).
  • Only where the fuse group is balanced (balancing: true): without a balancer nothing would hold the car (scheduling_not_available).
  • At most the provider's authorization window (Stripe: 7 days for an online card payment) less DRIVER_SCHEDULE_MARGIN_S (2 days) ahead (start_too_late): an authorization that expires before the capture loses the money (architecture §3.1). The page offers only the next 24 h.
  • If no car is plugged in within the plug-in window, or the driver starts now before plugging in, the 0 A is taken off the connector so the next car does not start paused.

items.title: A failed start is never silent (PRD §6)
items.text:
The consumer judges each session (Session.failed_start, cpms/consumer/README.md): it ended within a minute with 0 Wh, ended without energy after it was allowed current, delivered nothing for five minutes after it was allowed current (for a scheduled start: after start_at), or its outlet went Faulted under it. For every drop-in, scheduled or not:

  • the live page says so at once (it reads the session itself, every 3 s): "The charge did not start … unplug the cable, push it firmly in, and start again", or for a running session with no energy, what to check, with Stop;
  • the worker records it once (driver_failed_start, journaled) and e-mails the receipt address (driver_send_failed_start_mail, at least once, like the receipt);
  • the session settles as usual: 0 Wh cancels the reservation, no receipt.

A charge a fault stops after it has delivered (Jonas, 2026-11-06; the consumer's Session.interrupted_at) gets the same treatment, but is not a failed start: "The charge has stopped" on the page at once, with the re-plug advice and Stop, and one e-mail (driver_interrupted, driver_send_interrupted_mail). Nothing is stopped automatically. If the outlet leaves Faulted and the charge resumes, the page shows charging again; a second fault shows on the page but sends no second e-mail. The receipt follows as usual for the energy delivered.

Not reported to the driver: a session she stopped herself. Energy delivered later clears the session's state; the drop-in keeps the record that she was told. Right after the box starts a session the page shows "checking that the cable is locked" for DRIVER_LOCK_CHECK_S (15 s, architecture §3.1). Both numbers are provisional until they are measured on real hardware.

States: paying → authorized → starting → charging → ended (or starting → scheduled → charging, or scheduled → ended when cancelled), or abandoned (left the payment page, or DRIVER_CHECKOUT_TIMEOUT_S passed: the checkout is expired at the provider so it cannot be paid later), failed (declined, or the start failed), timed_out (no car, or the driver pressed Cancel). Every non-ended end releases any reservation; a payment that arrives after the drop-in gave up is recorded and released.

A second driver cannot pay for an outlet that is starting or charging; a driver on the payment page holds the outlet for three minutes.

items.title: The driver API (/api/driver/v1/, architecture §3.1)
items.text:
The contract for an organization's own driver front end (api.py): a django-ninja API of its own, with its own OpenAPI document (/api/driver/v1/openapi.json) and docs page (/api/driver/v1/docs), separate from the operator API. v1 changes only additively; state and payment.kind say they may grow. The served pages stay the reference client: both call the same actions, and a test runs one drop-in through each and compares the journal and the ledger.

Endpoint Credential What GET /outlets/{public_id} none, any origin the outlet by its QR id: site, charge point, live status, can_start, the ad hoc price incl. and excl. VAT (exact names the side the tariff states), the amount reserved, and scheduling (available here, how far ahead) GET /organizations/{key}/sites none, any origin the published sites and their public outlets, as the home page POST /outlets/{public_id}/start none {email, accept, language?, return_url?, start_at?} → 201 {token, session}; the session is payment_required with payment.checkout_url. accept must be true: the driver accepted the price and the reservation shown, as the served page's checkbox asks (422 price_not_accepted otherwise) GET /sessions/{id} session token the session, live: state (payment_required, starting, scheduled, charging, finishing, ended, failed_start, cancelled, failed), held, checking_cable, failed_start, interrupted, energy, power, cost, payment POST /sessions/{id}/cancel-payment session token the driver left the payment page POST /sessions/{id}/cancel session token give up before the car is in; a scheduled charge: stop it POST /sessions/{id}/start-now session token a scheduled charge: do not wait POST /sessions/{id}/stop session token stop charging GET /sessions/{id}/receipt session token the receipt, once captured (404 before)
  • The session token is the capability /s/<token> is: 24 random bytes, returned once by start, sent as Authorization: Bearer. {id} is the session's public id (DropIn.ref); a token reaches its own session only, and another id is a 404.
  • Refusals are errors with the codes the served pages translate: occupied, starting, offline, out_of_order, not_public, no_price, payments_not_set_up, payment_provider_unavailable, scheduling_not_available, start_too_late, return_url_not_allowed, invalid_email, invalid_language, too_many_requests, price_not_accepted (422; the served page shows the unticked box's message for it).
  • Allowed origins (cors.py). The public endpoints answer any origin. Start and the session endpoints answer a browser only from the organization's driver_origins (organization document; https, or http://localhost for development) and the hosts the instance serves the driver flow on itself (its driver_hosts, PUBLIC_BASE_URL, the named ALLOWED_HOSTS). The same list binds return_url for every caller: payment never returns to a page that is not the operator's. Payment returns to return_url with session=<id>&payment=done or payment=cancelled added; without it, to the served live page.
  • Rate limit. Start is limited per client address (an IPv6 /64), START_LIMIT (10 per 10 minutes), in front of the action, shared with the served page (cpms.core.limits: per process, enough to blunt abuse).
  • Not yet: the driver token, login and the account endpoints come with driver accounts (PRD §7, slice 5a); the subscription endpoints with the subscriber step.

items.title: Theme
items.text:
No project or customer branding is built in (architecture §14). The organization's name comes from the organization document; an optional theme block there sets an accent colour and a logo:

organization:
  key: demo
  name: Demo Laddning AB
  theme: {primary: "#0b7a3e", logo_url: "https://example.com/logo.svg"}

Both are validated by the manifest schema (hex colour, https URL), so nothing reaches the page's CSS unchecked. The return URL from the payment page uses the host the driver came in on, so an organization's own domain (charge.example.se pointed at the instance) stays its own through payment.

items.title: Design system
items.text:
Server-rendered Django templates + HTMX + Tailwind with daisyUI (PRD §5).

  • Partials. A page and its HTMX fragment are the same template: Django 6's template partials ({% partialdef panel inline %} and render(…, "driver/live.html#panel")). Small components are includes in templates/driver/components/ (price, stat, receipt, outlet header).
  • Tailwind without Node at runtime. scripts/build-css.sh downloads Tailwind's standalone CLI (a single binary with Tailwind built in, published by Tailwind Labs for exactly this) and daisyUI's two plugin files at pinned versions with checked SHA-256s into .tools/ (gitignored), and builds cpms/assets/app.css into cpms/static/cpms/app.css, which is committed. The server never builds CSS; it serves the committed file after collectstatic. Rebuild and commit after changing classes in a template. The same approach is the default in Phoenix (the tailwind hex package), in Rails (tailwindcss-rails) and in Django's django-tailwind-cli; daisyUI documents its use with the standalone CLI. Not thought through yet: nothing checks in CI that the committed CSS is up to date with the templates.
  • htmx 2.0.4 is vendored as cpms/static/vendor/htmx-2.0.4.min.js.
  • Mobile first: one column, max-w-md, tap targets of at least 48 px.

items.title: Not built yet
items.text: Spot-priced drop-in (needs the current spot price on the page), an EVSE id on the page and receipt (architecture §14, comes with the OCPI slice), driver accounts and the driver token (slice 5a), per-organization sender domains for mail (today: DEFAULT_FROM_EMAIL with the organization's name, and its e-mail as Reply-To).

items.title: Users and access
items.text:
How people and machines get into LeanCPMS, what each of them may do, and how an organization manages that itself. It is written for two readers: someone who wants to understand the model without reading code, and an organization's administrator who is about to manage their organization from the command line.

The worked example is LeanCPMS Cloud, the hosted instance run by Forsslund Systems AB. A self-hosted instance works the same way under its own host names; the differences are at the end. The examples use a made-up organization acme and addresses at example.com.

This describes the code as it is (leancpms-cli 0.1.4). The design and its reasons are in docs/architecture.md §3 and §11.

Contents

  1. Concepts
  2. On LeanCPMS Cloud
  3. The command line
  4. Common tasks
  5. Running your own instance

items.title: People
items.text:
A person is one e-mail address. There are no passwords and no user names. To log in to the portal you type your address, LeanCPMS e-mails you a short one-time code, and you type the code. Everything a person does, in the portal and on the command line, goes back to that one identity.

Nobody signs up. An address can log in only after someone has made it a member (below). An address that is not a member gets no code at all, not even an error message, so that the login page does not reveal who has an account.

items.title: The operator and organizations
items.text:
An instance holds several organizations. An organization is a company that owns charging stations: its sites, charge points, price list, sessions, receipts and monthly settlements belong to it, and it cannot see anyone else's.

The operator is whoever runs the instance. On LeanCPMS Cloud that is Forsslund Systems AB. The operator is not an organization; it stands above all of them and sees every organization.

items.title: Memberships and roles
items.text:
A membership connects a person to one organization, or to the operator. A person can have several: member of acme and of globex, say. Each membership has a role:

Role In the portal On the command line read (the default) sees everything about the organization gets keys that may only look write the same: the portal only reads, whatever the role gets keys that may also act: apply manifests, manage members and keys, stop sessions

So the role does not change what you see; it caps what the keys you get with cpms login may do (see Keys).

Each membership records who added it. Removing a person does not remove the members they added: when someone leaves, look at cpms members list and decide about the people they brought in.

items.title: The operator membership is the admin
items.text:
A membership without an organization is an operator membership. It is the instance's "superuser":

  • In the portal it shows every organization.
  • It is the only way into the Django admin pages at /admin/, which are a read-only view of every table (cpms/portal/admin_site.py).
  • With cpms login it can get an operator key, which reaches every organization and the operator-only commands (opening the gateway to unknown charge points, the organization document, the balancer).

Django's own is_staff and is_superuser flags decide nothing about access: nobody gets into /admin/ or sees an extra organization because of them, and they are never needed. Their one effect is protective: an organization's key cannot add, change or remove an account that has one of those flags, and losing a membership never switches such an account off (cpms/actions/members.py). Operator memberships are given by the operator only; an organization can never create one.

items.title: API keys
items.text:
Everything that is not a person in a browser talks to the instance's JSON API with an API key, sent as Authorization: Bearer <key>. The command line cpms is one such client.

A key looks like lcp_3f9a1c2e_<43 more characters>. The part after lcp_, here 3f9a1c2e, is its prefix: it is not secret, it names the key in lists and logs, and it is what you revoke. The rest is the secret. The instance stores only a hash of the whole key, so a key is shown exactly once, when it is made, and can never be shown again. Lose it and you make a new one.

Every key has three properties:

  • Who it is for. An organization key reaches one organization. An operator key reaches every organization and the operator-only commands.
  • Its scope. A read key may only look (HTTP GET). A write key may also act. A read key may do one thing besides looking: revoke itself (cpms logout).
  • Whose it is. A personal key belongs to a person: cpms login gets it after the person approved it in the portal, and it is named after the computer, such as cpms on anna-laptop. A machine key belongs to no person: it is made with cpms keys issue for a script, a CI pipeline, a dashboard or an agent, and it records which key issued it.

The rules that follow from that:

  • A role caps personal keys. A read member gets only read keys from cpms login. A write member may choose either.
  • A key never makes a wider key. An organization's write key may issue keys for its own organization, read or write; never an operator key, never a key for another organization. A read key issues nothing, and may not list keys or members either, since lists of keys and members are part of managing them.
  • Removing a member revokes their keys, and every key made from them. When a person loses a membership, their personal keys for it stop working, and so does every machine key issued with one of those keys, and every key issued with those, however far down. A personal key the person had already revoked (with cpms logout, say) still counts: the keys made from it go too.
  • Lowering a role does the same for write. Lowered from write to read, a member's personal write keys are revoked, together with every key issued from them, including read keys issued from them.
  • A switched-off account's keys stop working. A person whose last membership is removed is switched off: they can no longer log in, their portal login ends, and any personal key of theirs still left is refused.
  • Revoking one key revokes only that key. cpms keys revoke and cpms logout do not cascade: machine keys issued with the revoked key keep working. They still die with their maker's membership, as above.

The consequence to remember: a machine key lives only as long as the membership of the person whose key issued it. That is deliberate, so that nobody leaves behind working keys when they leave. A key for an integration that must keep working when people come and go is issued by the operator, from a key with no person in its chain (see Common tasks).

Who owns or issued a key, and who added a member, is shown as an e-mail address only to those who may see that person in the members list: the operator, and the organization the person is a member of now. Others see "operator" or "former member".

items.title: What each kind of key may do
items.text:
organization read key organization write key operator key Live state, sessions, events, monthly settlements own organization own organization every organization Export manifests, history, diff own organization own organization every organization Plan and apply the price list and site documents no own organization every organization Plan and apply the organization document no no yes Stop or close a session, rekey a charge point no own organization every organization OCPI connections look own organization every organization List, add, remove members, change roles no own organization's members (never an operator member) everyone List, issue, revoke keys no own organization's keys every key The gateway's admission window for unknown charge points (cpms admission) no no yes (opening it needs write) Revoke itself (cpms logout), cpms whoami yes yes yes

An operator key also has a scope: an operator read key looks at everything and changes nothing.

items.title: Other credentials
items.text:
These are not for people and not for the API, but they exist and it helps to know who handles them.

  • OCPI tokens. A roaming partner (an eMSP, or a registry such as Nobil) talks to the instance over OCPI with tokens of its own, one connection per organization and partner. cpms ocpi connect acme --name partner makes the connection and prints Token A once, to send to the partner; the partner registers, and the tokens are exchanged automatically. cpms ocpi disconnect ends it. An organization's write key may do this for its own organization; on LeanCPMS Cloud the operator usually does.
  • Charge point passwords. Each charge point declared with auth: basic in its site document has its own password for its OCPP connection. The gateway sets it on the box over OCPP; it is in no file and nobody sees it. cpms chargepoints rekey <key> replaces it.
  • Driver session tokens. A driver who pays by card at the QR code gets a link to their own session (/s/<token>). The token is the only key to that one charge. Drivers hold these; nobody at the organization needs them.
  • Instance secrets. The balancer's own operator key, the key between LeanCPMS and its gateway, the payment provider's keys: these live on the server and are the operator's (deploy/README.md).

items.title: The actions journal
items.text: Every change (adding a member, issuing or revoking a key, applying a manifest, approving a cpms login) writes a row to the actions journal: who, when, what, and the result. It never stores a secret or an e-mail address; it stores the key's prefix. That is what answers "who did this, and when" afterwards.

items.title: Host names
items.text:
Address For whom What https://portal.leancpms.com people the portal, the admin pages, and the page where you approve cpms login https://api.leancpms.com machines the JSON API (docs at /api/v1/docs), the command line, OCPI wss://ocpp.leancpms.com charge points the OCPP connection the organization's own domain, e.g. charge.example.com, or acme.leancpms.com drivers the station list, the QR pages and the driver API https://leancpms.com everyone the website, hosted apart from the instance

The portal and the admin pages answer only on portal.leancpms.com. Asked for on any other of the names, they redirect there, so a driver's domain never shows a login page. The API answers on api.leancpms.com; use that address with the command line.

items.title: How someone becomes a member
items.text:
There is no page for it. Members are added from the command line, or through the API it uses:

  1. The operator adds the organization's first administrator, with an operator key:

    cpms members add anna@example.com --org acme --role write

  2. That administrator adds colleagues, with their own personal write key:

    cpms members add ben@example.com --org acme              # read (the default)
cpms members add carla@example.com --org acme --role write

Nothing is e-mailed when a member is added. Tell the person yourself to go to https://portal.leancpms.com and log in with that address.

An organization can manage only its own members. It cannot see or change an operator member, and it learns nothing about a person's memberships elsewhere.

items.title: Logging in to the portal
items.text:
1. Open https://portal.leancpms.com.
  2. Type your e-mail address. A code is e-mailed to you; type it on the next page. If no mail comes, the address is not a member (or has a typo): ask whoever was to add you.
  3. With one organization you land on its overview; with several, on a list of them.

A login lasts 90 days on that browser, or until you log out (top right) or your last membership is removed. The portal shows, for each organization: an overview with live state, sessions, receipts and the monthly settlements. It only reads. Its texts follow the browser's language (Swedish or English).

Because the code goes to your e-mail, your mailbox is your password: whoever can read your mail can log in as you.

items.title: The admin pages
items.text: An operator member also sees an Admin button in the portal, which leads to https://portal.leancpms.com/admin/. Opened directly without a login, it sends you through the same code login first. Organization members get "403 Forbidden" there, whatever their role. The admin pages are read-only: changes are made with cpms and an operator key, never in the admin.

items.title: 3. The command line
items.text: cpms is a small program you install on your own computer. It talks to api.leancpms.com with your personal key. The examples assume a Unix shell (Linux or macOS).

items.title: Install
items.text:
leancpms-cli is published on PyPI, so it installs without access to the source repository. The recommended way is with uv, which also fetches Python 3.14 if your computer lacks it:

curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh     # if you do not have uv yet
uv tool install leancpms-cli
cpms --help
  • Upgrade: uv tool upgrade leancpms-cli. To pin a version: uv tool install leancpms-cli==0.1.4.
  • pipx works too, if Python 3.14 is already installed: pipx install leancpms-cli.
  • Other routes, for those with access to the repository while it is private: the wheel on the GitHub release (gh release download cli-v0.1.4 --repo forsslund/leancpms --pattern '*.whl', then uv tool install ./leancpms_cli-0.1.4-py3-none-any.whl), or straight from git (uv tool install "git+https://github.com/forsslund/leancpms#subdirectory=cli"). Both fail without repository access; PyPI does not.
  • Do not install it where the LeanCPMS server is installed: the server already contains cpms.

items.title: Log in: cpms login
items.text:
cpms login --url https://api.leancpms.com

This is the same "device login" as gh auth login:

  1. cpms asks the instance for a login and prints a page address and a code, such as KTRW-MZPB. It opens the page in your browser if it can (--no-browser only prints it, for a server over ssh).
  2. In the browser you land on portal.leancpms.com/portal/cli/. Log in with your e-mail code if you are not already logged in.
  3. The page shows the code, what asks for the key (cpms on <your computer's name>), when, and from which internet address. Check that the code is the one in your terminal. Approve only a login you just started yourself: whoever started it gets a key in your name.
  4. Choose the organization and what the key may do. A write member sees "may look and act (write)" and "may only look (read)"; a read member only the latter. --scope read on the command line preselects read.
  5. Approve. The terminal continues by itself and saves the key.

The code is valid for ten minutes and works once. Ten wrong codes in an hour lock the approval page for you for an hour.

The key is saved in the config file, ~/.config/cpms/config.toml, readable only by you:

[default]
url = "https://api.leancpms.com"
api_key = "lcp_3f9a1c2e_…"

Logging in again replaces the key in that profile; the old one keeps working until you revoke it (cpms keys revoke).

items.title: Profiles
items.text:
Each [name] in the config file is a profile: an address and a key. cpms login writes [default] unless you name another, and leaves the other profiles as they are. Pick a profile with --profile or the environment variable CPMS_PROFILE:

cpms login --url https://api.leancpms.com --profile acme-read --scope read
cpms --profile acme-read sessions --since 2026-11-01
CPMS_PROFILE=acme-read cpms sessions

Use one profile per organization if you are a member of several, since a personal key is for one organization.

Instead of a profile, a script can set CPMS_URL and CPMS_API_KEY in its environment. Without --profile, the environment wins over [default]. CPMS_CONFIG points at another config file. A command that finds no key exits with code 2 and says what to set.

items.title: cpms whoami and cpms logout
items.text:
$ cpms whoami
anna@example.com: write key 3f9a1c2e (cpms on anna-laptop) for organization acme

$ cpms logout
revoked key 3f9a1c2e
removed profile [default] from /home/anna/.config/cpms/config.toml

whoami says which key is in use: whose, for which organization, read or write. logout revokes the key in use on the server, then removes the profile. It revokes whatever key the profile holds, so never run it on a profile that holds an integration's machine key. A key from CPMS_API_KEY is revoked but stays in your environment; unset it.

items.title: Several computers
items.text: Run cpms login on each computer. Each gets its own personal key, named after the computer, so you can revoke one without touching the others. Do not copy the config file between computers: the same key in two places cannot be revoked in one of them only.

items.title: When a computer is lost or stolen
items.text:
The lost computer holds your personal key in ~/.config/cpms/config.toml, and perhaps a portal login in its browser.

  1. Secure your e-mail first. Whoever reads your mail can log in as you.

  2. Revoke the key. From another computer, log in (cpms login), then find the key named after the lost computer and revoke it:

    cpms keys list
# prefix    organization  scope  name                  personal (owner)  issued by         created ...
# 3f9a1c2e  acme          write  cpms on anna-laptop   anna@example.com  anna@example.com  ...
cpms keys revoke 3f9a1c2e

    Listing and revoking keys needs a write key. A read member asks a colleague with write, or the operator, to do it.

  3. Machine keys whose secrets were on that computer (in another profile, a script, a .env file) must be revoked too: revoking your personal key does not revoke keys issued from it.

  4. The portal login in its browser lasts up to 90 days and cannot be ended from elsewhere by you. The operator can end it by removing your memberships, which switches the account off, and adding you again. That also revokes your personal keys and every key issued from them, so decide first which machine keys must be issued anew. The portal only reads, but it shows sessions and receipts, which hold drivers' personal data.

items.title: Everyday commands
items.text:
Every command takes --json for machine-readable output and --profile. cpms <command> --help lists the rest.

Who is a member, and with which role

cpms members list
cpms members add ben@example.com --org acme                 # read
cpms members add carla@example.com --org acme --role write
cpms members set-role ben@example.com --org acme --role write
cpms members remove ben@example.com --org acme

--org acme is needed even though your key is already for acme. members list shows each member's role, whether the account is active, when they were added and by whom.

Keys

cpms keys list                                   # every key of the organization, revoked ones too
cpms keys issue --name dashboard --scope read    # prints the secret once
cpms keys revoke 7b2d90aa

keys issue makes a key for your own organization; the default scope is write, so say --scope read when looking is enough. The secret is printed on its own line on standard output, so it can go straight into a secret store: cpms keys issue --name ci --scope read > ci-key.txt.

Declared state: organization, price list, sites

These are YAML documents, kept best in a git repository of your own (cli/README.md, "A repository of manifests"):

cpms manifest export acme > all.yaml                  # every document
cpms manifest export acme --site main-street > sites/main-street.yaml
cpms manifest validate sites/main-street.yaml         # offline, needs no key
cpms manifest plan sites/main-street.yaml             # what would change; needs a write key
cpms manifest apply sites/main-street.yaml -m "Fused up to 50 A"
cpms manifest history acme --site main-street
cpms manifest diff acme --site main-street v3

apply shows the plan and asks before it applies; -m (the reason, stored with the version) is required. Removing anything needs --prune. An organization's key applies the price list and site documents; the organization document is changed by the operator.

Live state, sessions, the monthly settlements

cpms                                          # live state: sites, outlets, current per phase
cpms sessions --since 2026-11-01 --status ended
cpms sessions --since 2026-11-01 --csv > november.csv
cpms session SIM-0001/42                      # one session: <charge point>/<transaction>
cpms session SIM-0001/42 stop                 # acts at once, no confirmation
cpms report settlements --month 2026-10

items.title: Scripts, CI and agents
items.text: A script or an agent uses a machine key in CPMS_URL and CPMS_API_KEY, never on the command line, where it ends up in shell history and process lists. Exit codes: 0 ok, 1 the server said no or could not be reached, 2 usage or configuration. manifest apply never asks without a terminal: it prints the plan and exits 2 unless given --yes. More in cli/README.md, "For agents".

items.title: Add a colleague
items.text:
cpms members add ben@example.com --org acme      # or --role write to let them act

Then tell Ben to log in at https://portal.leancpms.com with that address, and, if he will use the command line, to install cpms and run cpms login --url https://api.leancpms.com.

items.title: Give or lower a role
items.text:
cpms members set-role ben@example.com --org acme --role write
cpms members set-role ben@example.com --org acme --role read

Raised to write, Ben runs cpms login again to get a write key; his read key stays as it was. Lowered to read, his write keys are revoked at once, and so is every key issued from them; the output lists their prefixes. Look at cpms keys list first if he made keys for integrations.

items.title: Remove someone
items.text:
cpms keys list                                   # first: which keys did they issue?
cpms members list                                # and whom did they add?
cpms members remove ben@example.com --org acme

This revokes Ben's personal keys for acme and every key issued from them, and lists the revoked prefixes. If it was his last membership his account is switched off and his portal login ends. The members he added stay: decide about them separately. Any integration running on a key Ben issued stops now; give it a new key first (next task).

items.title: A key for an integration that must outlive a person
items.text:
A dashboard, an accounting export, an agent: anything that should keep working when the person who set it up leaves.

A key issued with your personal key dies with your membership. Ask the operator instead, saying what it is for and whether it needs write.

The operator must issue it from a key with no person anywhere in its chain: a key made on the server with manage.py issue_key, or a key issued from such a key. A key the operator issues with their own personal operator key would in turn die with their operator membership. With such a person-free operator key in its environment, the operator runs:

cpms keys issue --org acme --name accounting-export --scope read

It appears in your cpms keys list with "operator" as its issuer (or nothing, if it was made directly on the server). Your organization can still revoke it.

If the integration may die with you (a script of your own, a test), issue it yourself:

cpms keys issue --name my-script --scope read

items.title: Revoke a key
items.text:
cpms keys list               # find its prefix
cpms keys revoke 7b2d90aa

It stops working at once. Only that key is revoked: keys issued from it keep working until revoked themselves, or until their maker's membership ends. An organization's write key may revoke any key of the organization: a colleague's personal key, a machine key, or one the operator issued for it. To revoke the key you are using yourself, run cpms logout.

items.title: 5. Running your own instance
items.text:
The model is the same; only the names and the first step differ.

  • The host names come from the server's settings: PORTAL_URL (where the portal and the admin answer; other hosts redirect there), PUBLIC_BASE_URL (the drivers' host in receipt links), each organization's driver_hosts in its organization document, and DJANGO_ALLOWED_HOSTS for every name. One name for everything works too: leave PORTAL_URL empty and every host serves the portal.

  • The first operator. Nobody can log in until someone is a member, so the first key comes from the server:

    sudo leancpms-manage issue_key --operator --name bootstrap   # prints an operator key once
CPMS_URL=https://cpms.example.com CPMS_API_KEY=lcp_… \
  cpms members add you@example.com --operator --role write
cpms login --url https://cpms.example.com                    # choose "Operator: every organization"

    Revoke the bootstrap key once you have your personal one, or keep it as the person-free key that issues integration keys.

  • Login codes are e-mailed through the SMTP server in the settings; in development without one, the mail is printed in the server's log (dev/README.md).

In the code: people and roles cpms/portal/models.py, cpms/portal/access.py; the admin cpms/portal/admin_site.py; member actions cpms/actions/members.py; key actions cpms/actions/keys.py and cpms/core/keys.py; cpms login cpms/actions/login.py, cpms/api/login.py, cpms/portal/cli.py, cpms/cli/login.py; scopes on every request cpms/api/auth.py.
